articles.title: Labor Mobilized for ‘Many vs. Mighty’ Midterms
articles.author: Jenny Brown
articles.content_excerpt: Something different was in the air as the labor movement mobilized for the midterms. More than usual, unions were willing to support insurgent candidates who refused corporate donations and bucked the Democratic Party establishment. They championed a Bernie Sanders-style list of working-class issues: Medicare for All, a higher minimum wage, union rights, immigrant rights, stopping war, and taxing the rich. Many are union members themselves. And they won. United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain called the election “the many versus the mighty.” In Michigan, the UAW was a key backer of the victorious Abdul El-Sayed, who earlier defeated the party’s depressing primary choice for U.S. Senate. “You had a lot of rich people who tried to… buy a seat, to buy these races,” Fain told Michigan Advanc

articles.title: ‘Delay, Deny, Discipline’ Is Amazon’s Real Pregnancy Policy, Workers Say
articles.author: Jenny Brown
articles.content_excerpt: Willamina Barclay was working as a picker at Amazon’s fulfillment center in Rochester, New York, when she felt lightheaded again. “She pleaded with a manager for a seat… He refused: ‘No, because you don’t have a [pregnancy] accommodation. If I give you a chair, I have to give everybody else a chair,’” he said, according to a recent lawsuit. But Barclay, who learned she was pregnant in March 2025, had already asked managers many times for accommodations—a seat, extra breaks to drink, eat, pee (or throw up) in the bathroom, no ladder-climbing or squatting, and no heavy lifting. Amazon—a company known for fast delivery—had failed to answer for weeks, demanding medical documentation. articles.title: The American Woman Who Joined Algeria’s Socialist Experiment
articles.author: Julia Harte
articles.content_excerpt: Within days of arriving in Algeria, months after its liberation from France in 1962, Elaine Klein knew she was there for the long haul. “The experiment to create a new socialist country from the impoverished colony, the tremendous task of building a state respected in the international arena, was daunting,” she later wrote. Yet, “My gut told me that I would settle here.” Her intuition was correct. For more than a decade, the Jewish New Yorker was the only American in Algeria’s new government. She assumed a range of roles — reporter, translator, envoy — as the former French colony established itself as an international haven for resistance groups, political dissidents, and anti-colonial organizers. articles.title: The Longest Hotel Strike in Washington State History
articles.author: Diana Varenik
articles.content_excerpt: You’d be forgiven for worrying, twelve weeks into a strike, that the boss is hell-bent on waiting you out. But after more than eighty days on the picket line at Seattle’s Embassy Suites by Hilton in Pioneer Square, Aspen Desmarais was undeterred. “I can live on a budget,” she said. “Been doing it since day one.” After eighty-five days, on September 10, workers won the longest hotel strike in Washington state history. Their union, UNITE HERE Local 8, represents four thousand hospitality workers in Oregon and Washington. Desmarais, a strike captain and bartender at the hotel, worked to keep others motivated throughout the fight. articles.title: Did Moderate Democrats Really Outperform the Left? No.
articles.author: Matt Bruenig
articles.content_excerpt: Democrats did well in the 2026 midterm elections. According to the current tally, they gained forty-one House seats , eight Senate seats , and five governorships . Democratic candidates of all types had success, making it difficult to easily point the finger at this or that faction for blowing the election. This has generated some frustration among factional partisans because such partisans are heavily invested in the idea that their style of politics is electorally superior to the politics of other factions. They can’t point to winners and losers to support their positions because, in this election, everyone was a winner. articles.title: Anthropic’s IPO Is a Bid to Manufacture Confidence
articles.author: Clark Randall
articles.content_excerpt: Anthropic, maker of artificial intelligence software Claude, is going public this Thursday. The initial public offering (IPO) could top the record SpaceX set earlier this year, once a concurrent private stock placement is counted. In February, Anthropic raised capital at a $380 billion valuation, and it is now seeking buy-in at $1.4 trillion. The rise has only been matched by the demand from investors, as Bloomberg reported the IPO road show was oversubscribed by six times the available shares. In other words, institutions will be crowding out individual investors vying for early gains. Anthropic aims to raise $64 billion from the IPO in a nontraditional coming-to-market event. articles.author: Pablo Castaño
articles.content_excerpt: In recent years, Pedro Sánchez’s Spanish government, formed by his Socialists (PSOE) and the left-wing alliance Sumar, has been a reference point for the global left. Rarely among social democratic politicians, Sánchez has become well-known for his confrontations with Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu, and for his governing coalition’s progressive social and economic policies. However, Spain’s government could soon fall into the hands of a new alliance of the conservative Partido Popular (PP) and the far-right Vox party. At least, this is what almost all polls now suggest, less than two weeks before the general election on November 29. articles.author: Randy Shaw
articles.content_excerpt: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The Power of Ongoing Outreach A big story behind the blue election tsunami was the sharp rise in youth voting. According to a leading source , youth turnout was 27% across the nation. It was 30% in battleground states. It was the best midterm youth turnout since 2018. Voters under 30 favored Democrats by a whopping 35%. In contrast, voters over 45 were almost equally divided. That’s why many believe “ the youth vote was key to Democratic Wins in the Midterms .” This sharp turnout increase among an historically under-performing demographic has been building for years.
